Trump diverges from NATO statement, emphasizing Ukraine mustn’t expand war
articles.summary: The US president’s unilateral tweak of a joint missive occurred days after Kyiv struck a Russian warship off the coast of Libya
articles.body: The U.S. president’s unilateral tweak of a joint missive occurred days after Kyiv struck a Russian warship off the coast of Libya. BRUSSELS — Donald Trump sprung a surprise on NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte after the two met in Florida amid the U.S. president's latest push to end the war between Ukraine and Russia. Following the Wednesday night meeting at Mar-a-Lago, the two leaders said they had "discussed the importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war, and the importance of obtaining a peaceful resolution to the war as rapidly as possible" in a joint statement shared by both the White House and NATO . Writing hours later on Truth Social , the president altered the tone of the remark by adding two words — changing the statement to say "Russia and Ukraine" must avoid such actions. A NATO official, who was granted anonymity to speak freely about the sensitive issue, said the original missive was the officially agreed statement between the two sides — signaling Trump had later amended the statement unilaterally. The addition is pointed, coming days after Ukraine struck a Russian warship in a Libyan port, thousands of kilometers from Kyiv. The attack, which legal experts say may have broken international law , has drawn no criticism from most of Ukraine's allies given Russia's daily bombardment against its neighbor. It also highlights persistent tensions between Trump and Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the Ukrainian leader who has refused to abandon Kyiv's long-range strikes against Russian refineries and critical infrastructure. Trump last month said it was "time for Ukraine to get a new President" — blaming Zelenskyy for holding up a peace deal. That posture marks a contrast to Trump's recent overtures toward Russian President Vladimir Putin, whom he referred to as a "friend" during last week's trilateral meeting with the Kremlin boss and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen. Russian strikes have, for years, continuously targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure. The updated language also throws up a fresh challenge for Rutte. The former Dutch prime minister has repeatedly lavished praise on the American president in public as he scrambles to maintain U.S. arms shipments and limited support for Ukraine, and unity inside NATO. But the divergence showcases how his approach to keep Trump on message has clear limits. Despite the Truth Social addition pointing to Ukraine, Trump later added he had "spent a lot of time talking about the fact that I would like to see President Putin pull back all Military aggression against territories throughout Europe" during the meeting. Attention will now turn to a NATO foreign ministers meeting in Brussels on Dec. 2, which allies had previously expected to line up with a long-anticipated U.S. review of its troop presence in Europe. The U.S. has since told allies the revamp would be delayed . The Trump-Rutte meeting was originally intended to center around the overhaul, dubbed the Europe Posture Review, the NATO official said, but instead focused on transatlantic defense industrial scale-up and Russian hybrid attacks in Europe as the review's publication was postponed.

articles.title: Rwanda return hubs in focus as higher Interior Ministry budget accepted
articles.body:
Plans foreseeing a rise of €1 billion ($1.1 billion) in the budget for the Interior Ministry have been approved by the three parties in Germany's coalition government, after much debate centering on something that makes up a relatively small proportion of that money: the controversial planned centers for rejected asylum seekers in Rwanda.

According to Klaus-Peter Willsch of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU), just €5 million are earmarked for the so-called return hubs, shared between several European countries.

He said the €20 million that has often been cited as being for the Rwanda migration centers was not only for the hubs in that country, but for other potential projects in third countries as well.

Despite the relatively small amounts of money involved, the Rwanda plans devised by Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU) along with Austria, Denmark, the Netherlands and Greece came under fire not only from coalition partners the Social Democrats (SPD) but particularly from opposition parties.

The Green Party and the Left Party both rejected the idea for ethical reasons, with Green lawmaker Leon Eckert speaking of "state-organized human trafficking," while Dietmar Bartsch of the Left pointed out that the deal was being made with an authoritarian regime.

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), for its part, said it found the plans too soft, with parliamentarian Marcus Bühl calling them a "smoke screen," as just 20 rejected asylum-seekers from Germany were to be initially sent to Rwanda under the scheme.

Dobrindt defended the scheme, saying that the opposition was trying to stir up controversy about a concept that had been approved at European level. He also called criticism of the political system in Rwanda inappropriate, citing a school for Afghan girls that had been set up in the country amid the ban on secondary education for females by the Taliban government.

The interior minister also praised the additional funds given to his ministry as a contribution to Germany's defense against hybrid attacks from Russia, with a rise in the budgets of both the IT security and the civic protection departments.

The draft 2027 budget, which was approved by the conservative CDU/CSU bloc and the SPD, however includes less funding for the BAMF migration authority (from €999 million in 2026 to €994 million) and for integration aid for migrants and refugees (down €328 million to €1.07 billion).

German Foreign MinisterJohann Wadephul has warned against an expansion of the Ukraine conflict into other regions after the Ukrainian attacks on Russian ships in Libya.

"Ukraine's ​right to self-defense is undisputed and we ​do support Ukraine, but I strongly ⁠warn ​against allowing ​this conflict to spread ​geographically," he ‌said at ​a ⁠press conference in Berlin with ⁠his ​Romanian counterpart Dan Neculaescu.

Wadephul also condemned reported Russian attacks on two foreign freight ships said to be carrying grain near Ukraine's Black Sea port of Odesa, saying such attacks did not concern only the security of nearby nations but also the food security of people in the Global South.

"It is clear that we cannot accept drone attacks on trading vessels," he said. "NATO will therefore step up its engagement in the region."

articles.title: Trial of alleged Russian spy delayed over health issues
articles.body:
The trial of a German-Ukrainian woman due to go on trial on Thursday on charges of spying for Russia was delayed in the morning after the accused developed health problems that required treatment by emergency medical workers, a spokeswoman for a Berlin court said.

It was not clear whether her trial could go ahead as planned.

The 57-year-old woman has been accused of passing information to an officer from Russia's GRU intelligence agency who was posing as a diplomat at the Russian Embassy in Berlin.

Prosecutors allege that she used contacts with current and former German Defense Ministry officials to collect information on military aid for Ukraine, drone test sites and the arms industry.

She also faces accusation of having provided her alleged handler access to key political events in Berlin.

The woman was arrested in late January, with the alleged involvement of the Russian Embassy causing considerable outrage in Berlin.

Russia's ambassador was summoned over the incident, and the handler — identified by news weekly Der Spiegel as the embassy's deputy military attache — was expelled from Germany.

articles.title: Trump downplays Russia, China support for Iran during talks with US troops
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has downplayed Russia and China’s support for Iran, dismissing the significance of their reported intelligence-sharing with Tehran while threatening renewed military action against the country.

Speaking to reporters at his Mar-a-Lago residence in Florida on Thanksgiving, Trump said direct military participation, rather than intelligence-sharing, would constitute meaningful involvement in the war.

“They could get involved, but involvement to me would mean shooting, not giving them little information,” he said.

Trump also claimed Iran possessed missiles capable of reaching Europe and said Washington was still giving Tehran an opportunity to negotiate a deal. He added that he had spoken to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in recent days.

During calls with US military personnel deployed across the Middle East, including in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, Trump praised their role in the war on Iran.

His remarks came amid escalating regional tensions, with Kuwait reporting on Thursday that an Iranian drone attack killed two Italian workers. Tehran denied involvement.

articles.title: UK minister condemns drone attack on Kuwait that killed two Italian nationals
articles.body:
Stephen Doughty, UK minister of state for the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, has condemned the drone attack against Kuwait that killed two Italian nationals.

“These reckless attacks are utterly unacceptable,” Doughty said in a post on X.

“The UK stands firmly with Kuwait, Italy and all those affected,” he added.

We condemn today’s drone attacks against Kuwait, which tragically resulted in the deaths of two Italian nationals and in further injuries. These reckless attacks are utterly unacceptable.

The UK stands firmly with Kuwait, Italy and all those affected.@ukinkuwait @UKinItaly

articles.title: Trump says US has ‘victory at hand’ in war on Iran, offers Tehran chance for deal
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump says Washington has “victory at hand” in its war on Iran and is giving Tehran an opportunity to reach an agreement that could prevent further loss of life.

Speaking during a Thanksgiving call with US military personnel from his Mar-a-Lago residence in Florida, Trump suggested that the timing of victory remained his decision.

“It’s going to be whenever I want it to be, to be honest,” he said.

Trump also said his administration was still offering Iran an opening to negotiate.

“We’re trying to be nice. We’re giving them every chance to make a deal and save a lot of lives, but I’m not sure if they are gonna take advantage of that,” he said.

“Some people question why. Are they crazy? Maybe they are.”

The remarks come amid continued uncertainty over efforts to reach an agreement to end the US-Israel war on Iran.

articles.title: Iran’s Araghchi sees opportunities for ‘peace diplomacy’ after war
articles.body:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says an end to the US-Israel war on Iran could pave the way for renewed diplomacy, economic development and international cooperation.

“With the consolidation of the Iranian people’s victories against the enemies of this land and the end of the recent imposed war, peace diplomacy can undoubtedly open new horizons and valuable opportunities,” Araghchi said in a message marking Isfahan Day, according to the IRNA news agency.

Araghchi accused the US and Israel of targeting Iran’s industrial and defence infrastructure, as well as damaging historical monuments and cultural heritage sites during the two recent wars.

He also highlighted the potential for post-war economic recovery, saying tourism and cultural exchanges could stimulate economic growth, expand cross-border cooperation and strengthen international relations.

The foreign minister did not announce any new diplomatic initiative or timetable for ending the war.

articles.title: Araghchi holds call with Italian FM over ‘suspicious’ attack on Kuwait
articles.body:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has “expressed condolences over the deaths of Italian citizens in Kuwait” in phone calls with his Italian and Kuwaiti counterparts.

“The incident is suspicious and looks like a pre-cooked recipe for war,” he said in a post on X, adding that Iran stands ready to cooperate with Kuwait and Italy to determine the cause of the incident.

Earlier, Araghchi said he expressed his condolences over the death of the two Italian nationals in a phone call with his Italian counterpart Antonio Tajani, categorically denying Iranian involvement in the attack.

articles.title: Trial of Berlin woman accused of spying for Russia begins after delay
articles.summary: The trial of a German-Ukrainian woman charged with spying for Russia began in Berlin
articles.body:
The trial of a German-Ukrainian woman charged with spying for Russia began in Berlin.

The start of the proceedings was delayed in the morning after the accused developed health problems that required treatment by emergency medical workers, a spokeswoman for a Berlin court said.

Later, however, she was brought into the courtroom in a wheelchair, wearing dark sunglasses.

Several times throughout the afternoon, the defense attorneys said their client was feeling nauseous, and a bucket was brought in. A doctor was present in the courtroom.

The trial is expected to last until May 2027.

articles.title: Russia says EU budget plans would prolong war in Ukraine
articles.summary: Russia has criticized the European Union's proposed seven-year budget, accusing the bloc of seeking to prolong the war in Ukraine
articles.body:
Russia has criticized the European Union's proposed seven-year budget, accusing the bloc of seeking to prolong the war in Ukraine.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the EU's plans to allocate money for Ukraine in its budget would make Kyiv "less inclined toward a peace process and more determined to continue the war."

Peskov said the result would be more military spending, leaving less for governments to spend on school, hospitals and social facilities.

"This is not money for peace," Peskov said.

Support for Ukraine is among the key areas of discussion in the 2028-2034 budget which includes up to €100 billion for Ukraine, however diplomats say this figure falls well short of Kyiv's needs.

articles.title: Germany: 2 arrested, suspected of plotting synagogue attack
articles.summary: Officers from Germany's federal criminal police force carried out the arrests
articles.body: Germany 's federal prosecutor's office on Thursday said it had ordered the arrest of two Iraqi citizens in Germany who are believed to be members of a pro- Iranian terrorist group. It identified the men as Mostafa Al-R. and Ameer J., and said that they were arrested in Heidelberg in Baden-Württemberg in the southwest, and in Cologne , several hours' drive to the north. Officers from Germany's federal criminal police force carried out the arrests. Prosecutors also announced searches and raids of 17 sites in total across three separate states, saying these were ongoing. After two suspects were arrested, Hendrik Wüst, the premier of North Rhine-Westphalia , thanked the security agencies for their vigilance and dedication. "Protecting Jewish life is our shared responsibility," he wrote on X. "Jewish life must be able to flourish freely and safely in our country. Anyone who attacks it attacks us all," Wüst added. Prosecutors said the two men were "strongly suspected" of membership in a domestic terrorist organization. They said that Mostafa Al-R. wa an associate of a man in the US known as Mohammad Al-Saadi, who is accused of setting up a group with the acronym HAYI (Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiyya) that is thought to be "responsible for a series of attacks against US, Israeli and Jewish institutions in Europe from March 2026," in the aftermath of the outbreak of Donald Trump's war with Iran . Mostafa Al-R. and Al-Saadi allegedly "founded a separate organization to prepare and carry out further attacks in Germany and Europe at the end of 2025." Prosecutors say Ameer J. joined this group. It gathered funds and "recruited several external people to carry out explosive attacks." "On the group's orders, unknown assailants headed on two consecutive nights in late March 2026 — presumably with explosives — to synagogues in Cologne and in one other European city," prosecutors wrote. "The plan was, for reasons as yet unknown, ultimately not carried out." Prosecutors said that intelligence behind the arrests could be traced back to the federal domestic intelligence agency , the BfV. More than 250 police officers from various forces were part of Thursday's operation. Both suspects were expected to appear before judges later on Thursday for a decision on them being placed in investigative detention. One other person is being sought as part of the investigation, with several others not currently suspected of criminal offenses affected by it. The stated date for the plot to attack Cologne's synagogue, late March this year, would have roughly coincided with a series of crimes in Europe targeting Jewish people or institutions in the weeks after the outbreak of war with Iran. These included an explosion in front of Liege synagogue in Belgium on March 9 , which caused property damage but no injuries. Police in the Netherlands investigated a fire at Rotterdam's synagogue a few days later . An explosive device was set off outside a Jewish school in Amsterdam soon after , prompting heightened security across the Netherlands. In London, a Jewish ambulance service was targeted in arson attacks in March , not long before two Jewish men were stabbed in broad daylight in what investigators treated as a likely act of terrorism. Several months later, in September, police in Wuppertal in Germany arrested an Afghan national on suspicion of trying to set a fire at the city's synagogue.

articles.title: Israeli settlers damage Palestinian family’s homes in West Bank attack
articles.summary: It added that the concrete foundations of the homes had been partially broken
articles.body: Israeli settlers have smashed the foundations of two homes belonging to a Palestinian family in the occupied West Bank after attacks stopped the family from returning. Security cameras showed the settlers bringing a bulldozer to the two-storey houses in the village of Jaloud, near Nablus, at about 1am on Thursday (23:00 GMT on Wednesday), before starting to damage them, Reuters reported. It added that the concrete foundations of the homes had been partially broken. “This latest escalation is a direct consequence of the lack of law enforcement and the sense of impunity enjoyed by the perpetrators,” said Ghiath Nasser, the owners’ lawyer. The Israeli military said the attack was “a serious criminal act” and said it was investigating, despite settlers remaining in the vicinity throughout the day. The Tubasi family now live in a small house in Jaloud with a direct view of the homes they fled. “They want to demolish the houses so that we cannot return to them,” Wael Tubasi, one of the owners, said. “Even though there is a court order, and the army is required to remove them from the area entirely, not just return us to our homes, it’s still not being implemented,” he said. The family said settlers set up a tent near their homes in April and began attacking them. They said settlers set fire to the homes, cut their water and electricity and blocked the roads. After three months, settlers told the family they had an hour to leave or be killed “like the Dawabsheh family”, Wael’s mother, Aedah, said. In 2015, settlers set fire to the Dawabsheh family’s home in the village of Duma, killing an 18-month-old child and both his parents. In September, soldiers escorted the family back to their homes under the court order. Ten minutes later, about 200 settlers attacked them, forcing the family and the soldiers to retreat, the family said. The settlers then burned the homes and broke much of the furniture. “I’m forbidden from reaching my home, while the settlers have the right to remain inside. What rights are there?” Aedah said. The attack follows weeks of settler pogroms across the occupied West Bank. There have been an average of 53 settler attacks a week since the start of the year, according to the UN. The agency said on November 20 that more than 400 settler attacks causing casualties or damage had been recorded since September, more than in any previous season . Over the weekend, settlers set fire to at least a dozen vehicles and several homes in five villages, and sprayed “Revenge” on walls. Last week, settlers killed an elderly Palestinian woman and wounded 10 other people in a pogrom near Jericho . According to the Israeli rights group Yesh Din, 93.6 percent of investigations into settler pogroms are closed without indictments.

Muslim World League ‘strongly condemns’ Houthi attack on Saudi oil refinery
articles.summary: The Muslim World League (MWL) has “strongly condemned” an attack on an oil refinery in Saudi Arabia’s Jazan region
articles.body:
The Muslim World League (MWL) has “strongly condemned” an attack on an oil refinery in Saudi Arabia’s Jazan region.

The attack, which killed one worker and injured several others, temporarily halted some operations at the plant.

The Saudi-led military coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis said that the Iranian-backed group had attacked the refinery.

“The Muslim World League has strongly condemned the continued sinful aggression by the terrorist Houthi militia against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia,” the group said in a statement.

MWL Secretary-General Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulkarim Al Issa said the attacks “violate all religious values, as well as international and humanitarian laws and norms, and confirm the criminal approach of this terrorist militia in deliberately targeting civilians and civilian facilities”, adding that the league stands in full solidarity with Saudi Arabia.

articles.title: ‘Difficult to believe Iranian denials’ over deadly Kuwait drone attack
articles.body:
Mohamad Bazzi, director of the Center for Near Eastern Studies at New York University, says it is hard to believe Iran’s denials that it was behind a deadly drone attack on Kuwait.

“They [Iran] have consistently targeted Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and other countries in the Gulf and so it is difficult to believe these denials,” he told Al Jazeera.

Bazzi said he believed that the Iranians were “surprised” that there were foreign casualties in the attack and were now trying to de-escalate the situation.

“This seems to be an attempt from Iran to de-escalate the situation and try to avoid blame and especially to avoid any potential Italian response or potential EU response – not a military response per se but a higher level condemnation from the EU for this attack,” Bazzi said.

articles.title: Deadly attack on Saudi refinery raises tensions as fighting escalates in Yemen
articles.body:
An attack on Saudi Arabia’s Jazan oil refinery has killed a Nepali worker, injured several others and disrupted operations, as fighting between the Saudi-led coalition and Yemen’s Houthis intensifies.

Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Energy said an aerial projectile struck the facility on Thursday, sparking a fire and forcing a temporary suspension of some operations.

The ministry did not identify who carried out the attack, but the Saudi-led coalition blamed the Houthis and warned that further strikes on civilian infrastructure would be met with a military response.

The coalition later claimed to have destroyed a Houthi missile launch platform in Yemen’s Hodeidah governorate.

Meanwhile, Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces reported hundreds of strikes against Houthi positions, claiming to have killed or wounded scores of fighters.

The escalating violence is worsening Yemen’s humanitarian crisis, with the UN reporting more than 360,000 people displaced since August.

articles.title: Botchorishvili Denies Discussions on Moving Russia Talks to Moscow or Tbilisi, Kobakhidze Says It’s a Possibility
articles.summary: Georgian Dream Foreign Minister Maka Botchorishvili says there's no agreement on moving the resumed Russia-Georgia dialogue to Moscow or Tbilisi
articles.body: Georgian Dream Foreign Minister Maka Botchorishvili says there's no agreement on moving the resumed Russia-Georgia dialogue to Moscow or Tbilisi, while Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze said such a thing is possible after the Belarusian foreign minister suggested the talks may move to the "capitals" after the first meeting took place in Minsk. The remarks follow a November 19 meeting in Minsk, Belarus, between George Zurabashvili, Georgia’s first deputy foreign minister and newly appointed special representative for relations with Russia, and Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin. Following the meeting, Belarusian Foreign Minister Maxim Ryzhenkov suggested that the talks could move to Moscow and Tbilisi, citing "substantive negotiations" during the first meeting. Botchorishvili: No Proposal or Decision Speaking to Georgia’s Public Broadcaster on November 25, Botchorishvili said there was "neither a proposal nor a decision" to hold meetings in Moscow or Tbilisi and that the issue was not on the agenda, adding that she did not consider it appropriate to discuss such matters in advance. She also dismissed Ryzhenkov’s assessment that the Minsk meeting had resulted in significant progress in building mutual trust between Georgia and Russia. “The Belarusian side is not a party to these meetings and has no information about their substance or results,” Botchorishvili said, stressing that only Georgia and Russia could assess the outcome of the talks. “Whether further meetings are necessary or whether they should continue is for the parties to decide, not those who have no role in the substance or conduct of these meetings." 26/11/2026 - Kobakhidze Suggests Russia’s Import Restrictions May Be Linked With ‘Deep State’ While acknowledging Belarus’ role in facilitating the Minsk meeting, Botchorishvili stressed that no agreement had been reached on further talks. “There is no agreement whatsoever on the continuation of meetings or on further steps. If there is a need for another meeting, the parties will discuss where it would be best to hold it, taking into account the circumstances and specific needs,” she said. Asked whether Minsk would replace Prague as the venue for Georgian-Russian talks, Botchorishvili said no decision had been made on a permanent location. “It is not written anywhere that the meeting must necessarily take place in Prague or any other city. Minsk was proposed as the venue, and, of course, we had no objection to holding the meeting there. This changes nothing about the substance of the meeting,” she said. Kobakhidze: Meetings in Moscow and Tbilisi Pose No Risks Talking to journalists on November 26, Kobakhidze said meetings could take place in both Moscow and Tbilisi, arguing that holding talks in the two capitals would not undermine Georgia’s non-recognition policy toward occupied Abkhazia and South Ossetia. “These meetings can, of course, also take place in Moscow and Tbilisi. If such an approach is adopted, it is fundamentally important that the meetings be held alternately in Moscow and Tbilisi,” Kobakhidze told reporters. Kobakhidze stressed that the format should not entail any risks concerning the non-recognition policy of Georgia's occupied territories or other issues. “Holding these meetings in Moscow and Tbilisi does not pose any risks,” he said. “The main thing is that not even a single gesture should cast a shadow over the non-recognition policy. Neither the placement of flags there nor the holding of meetings in Moscow and Tbilisi runs counter to the principle of non-recognition.” Renewed Russia-Georgia Dialogue The informal direct dialogue between Georgia and Russia, commonly known as the Abashidze-Karasin format, was launched in late 2012, with Tbilisi introducing the post of a “Special Representative for Relations with Russia” for that purpose. In its original design, the format was limited to addressing trade, economic, humanitarian, and cultural issues, as diplomatic relations remain cut off amid Russia’s continued occupation of Georgian territories and its recognition of Abkhazia and Tskhinvali/South Ossetia as “independent states.” George Zurabashvili was appointed as Georgian Dream Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze’s special representative for relations with Russia on October 21, filling a position that had been vacant since December 2025. He was also allowed to retain his post as the first deputy foreign minister. Zurabashvili’s appointment raised concerns among former Georgian diplomats, who warned of a “dangerous trend” and questioned whether the move could signal a de facto restoration of diplomatic relations with Moscow, while also pointing to what they saw as the expansion of the post’s limited mandate to include security issues as well. articles.title: Rama Responds to Protests With New Restrictions Ahead of Nationwide Demonstration: SP Approve Hefty Fines Despite Constitutional Court Ruling Against Them
articles.summary: The court partially upheld the complaint and said it would issue a final ruling soon
articles.body: Two days before a nationwide demonstration called by students and activists, Albania’s ruling Socialist majority approved legislation restricting the right to protest, introducing tougher penalties that could leave demonstrators facing both legal and financial consequences, even when taking part in peaceful gatherings. The protest has been called for November 28, a date of particular symbolic significance in Albania: the 114th anniversary of the country’s declaration of independence. However, as parliament debated the new legislation, it came as a breaking news that Albania’s Constitutional Court ruled against the fines and announced that it would fast-track its review of a complaint filed by students and opposition lawmakers. The court partially upheld the complaint and said it would issue a final ruling soon. But the ruling Socialists said they would press ahead with the legislative changes despite the Constitutional Court’s decision. The government adopted two emergency acts on October 28, 2026, amid a wave of mass demonstrations that have repeatedly erupted into clashes with police. Normative Act amends Albania’s Law on Public Gatherings, granting the State Police broader powers to intervene in demonstrations and prohibit protests. It also introduces administrative fines ranging from 10,000 to 500,000 Albanian lek (approximately $120 to $6,200). Albania is experiencing one of its most politically tense periods in more than a decade. Protests against Prime Minister Edi Rama’s government, which began in late May, have continued almost daily in the capital, Tirana, for nearly six months. The demonstrations initially emerged in opposition to a luxury tourism development planned in Zvërnec, on Albania’s southern coast, by a group of investors led by Jared Kushner, the American businessman and son-in-law of US President Donald Trump. The project has drawn criticism because of its location in an environmentally protected coastal area. What began as a campaign against the development gradually expanded into a broader protest movement, attracting people angered by the rising cost of living, government arrogance, a lack of accountability and systemic corruption. The demonstrations intensified in October, when students joined the protests and began demanding Rama’s resignation. By mid-October, students had become a central force in the movement. They are demanding better conditions at public universities, lower tuition fees and meaningful action against corruption, which they say extends far beyond the education system. Many young protesters say they see little room for opportunity under Rama’s government and increasingly struggle to imagine a future for themselves in Albania. As confrontations escalated, police used force against students, including water cannons, tear gas and rubber bullets, in attempts to disperse demonstrations. Rama has refused to resign, despite continuing demands from protesters. Instead, his government has moved to tighten the legal framework governing public demonstrations. The prime minister has defended the changes as necessary to maintain public order and protect businesses affected by violence during protests. Journalists, activists and government critics, however, argue that the legislation risks being used to suppress a broader protest movement challenging the government at a politically sensitive moment. Under the amendments, police can prohibit or restrict demonstrations for up to three days in areas surrounding a wide range of public institutions. The Police can impose restrictions within designated areas around government buildings, educational institutions and healthcare facilities if authorities believe there is a risk of violence against people or damage to property. The restriction can be renewed for another three days, meaning a demonstration could effectively be banned for up to six consecutive days. Organizers have the right to challenge such decisions before an administrative court. However, a controversial provision means that even if the court rules in their favor, the police are not required to immediately implement the judgment. In practice, critics warn, the changes could make it considerably harder to organize demonstrations, including peaceful ones, because restrictions can be imposed on the basis of police assessments that a gathering might turn violent. In Tirana, where government offices, shcools, hospitals and major transport hubs are spread across the city, the restricted perimeters could potentially cover substantial parts of the capital. If officers identify social media posts they believe encourage violence in connection with the organization of a demonstration, they can demand that the content be removed and not repeated. The provision raises concerns about how the authorities will distinguish between genuine incitement to violence and legitimate political speech, criticism of the government or calls for peaceful demonstrations. Critics argue that the legislation gives police considerable discretion in determining what constitutes an online call for violence. The amendments significantly increase administrative penalties, with some fines reportedly rising by as much as tenfold compared with previous levels. According to the text of the legislation published by Albanian media, fines range from 10,000 to 500,000 lek, more than 5500 euros and eight times albanian middle wage. This means that participation in a demonstration could carry substantial financial risks, even in the absence of physical violence. The legislation has drawn criticism from activists, civil society organizations and opposition parties. Student groups, civil society organizations and opposition lawmakers have petitioned Albania’s Constitutional Court, asking it to repeal the amendments and suspend their implementation until a final ruling is issued. The Court ruled to suspend the article regarding fines for blocking roads. The court announced that it would fast-track its review of a complaint filed by students and opposition lawmakers. The court partially upheld the complaint and said it would issue a final ruling soon. More than 100 peaceful demonstrators have already been fined under the new legislation, according to Albanian media reports. Police have also initiated criminal proceedings against a large number of people, including minors.

articles.title: European Parliament adopts resolution on Georgia, calls for sanctions and release of political prisoners
articles.summary: The European Parliament reiterated its call for a coordinated EU response
articles.body: The European Parliament adopted a resolution on Georgia on November 26, calling for the immediate release of political prisoners and the imposition of targeted sanctions against senior Georgian officials. The resolution, titled “Case of Paata Burchuladze and political prisoners under the Georgian Dream regime,” was approved with 441 votes in favor, 47 against and 86 abstentions. The European Parliament reiterated its call for a coordinated EU response, including targeted sanctions and visa bans against individuals it holds responsible for serious human rights violations, specifically naming Georgian Dream founder Bidzina Ivanishvili, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili and Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze, alongside other senior officials, judges, prosecutors and law enforcement personnel. MEPs condemned the sentences handed down to Paata Burchuladze, Irakli Nadiradze and Paata Manjgaladze, demanding their immediate and unconditional release, along with all individuals the resolution identifies as political prisoners or unlawfully detained. The document urges the Georgian authorities to uphold international fair trial standards, guarantee Burchuladze adequate medical care and legal assistance, facilitate regular communication with his family and ensure unrestricted consular access. The European Parliament further calls on the Georgian authorities to end what it describes as politically motivated prosecutions and judicial harassment of artists, opposition figures, journalists and activists, while guaranteeing freedom of expression, assembly and association. MEPs also demand independent investigations into allegations of excessive use of force, intimidation and ill-treatment of protesters, stressing the need to hold those responsible accountable. The resolution reaffirms the European Parliament’s support for the Georgian people and their democratic aspirations, emphasizing that respect for the rule of law, the European Convention on Human Rights and fundamental freedoms is essential for progress toward EU membership. MEPs also criticized the failure of some EU member states to take action against individuals they consider responsible for democratic backsliding in Georgia.

articles.title: Dodik after the Decision of the Constitutional Court: They Will Not Put Up a Single Flag of the Army of RBiH in RS
articles.summary: This is a constitutional right of the Serb people and Republika Srpska
articles.body: Milorad Dodik, president of the SNSD party, said that “not even 100 Constitutional Courts” will put up a single flag of the Army of RBiH in Republika Srpska, after the Constitutional Court ruled that the ban on displaying Army of RBiH insignia in the Criminal Code of Republika Srpska is unconstitutional. “If 100 Constitutional Courts appear, not a single one will put up the flag of the Army of RBiH in Republika Srpska; I dare them to try,” Dodik said at the press conference, RTRS reported. “This is a constitutional right of the Serb people and Republika Srpska. The will of the Serb people cannot be challenged,” Dodik said, adding that “there is no getting over this.” He called the decision of the Constitutional Court “a typical Muslim conspiracy theory to destroy Republika Srpska.” At the plenary session held on November 19 and 20, the Constitutional Court of BiH ruled that the Criminal Code of Republika Srpska is unconstitutional for criminalizing the public display, representation, and use of symbols and insignia that promote or glorify the Army of RBiH. Previously, the US filed an appeal regarding this ban, and the member of the Presidency of BiH, Denis Bećirović, submitted a request for a constitutionality assessment. In the same session, the Constitutional Court rejected the statement by Željka Cvijanović, the Serb member of the BiH Presidency, that Republika Srpska’s vital interest had been violated. It also rejected the decision by the National Assembly of Republika Srpska confirming that statement. Cvijanović vetoed the Decision of the Presidency of BiH to appoint members of the Commission for the Preservation of National Monuments, which had been made without consensus. This decision of the Presidency remains in force. The National Assembly of Republika Srpska banned displaying insignia of the Army of RBiH by amending the Criminal Code. The Constitutional Court of Republika Srpska has previously assessed that this law did not violate the vital national interest of the Bosniak people, N1 writes.

articles.summary: The disaster claimed 27 lives, while one person remains missing
articles.body: BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 27. Authorities in the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC) have detained another suspect as part of the investigation into the sinking of the FiloJet high-speed catamaran late this summer. The disaster claimed 27 lives, while one person remains missing. The tenth suspect was taken into custody at the port of Famagusta. A court has ordered that he remain in detention for one day. Nine people were previously arrested in connection with the incident in August, including the catamaran's captain, seven crew members, and the head of ferry operator Filo Denizcilik. The latest detention marks the first new arrest since the disaster. An analysis and decoding of data from the vessel's onboard recorder revealed that the catamaran's captain, Mustafa Öz, had obtained his ferry operator's license in Honduras by paying $3,500. The fiberglass FiloJet catamaran sank on August 30 while sailing from Kyrenia in the TRNC to the port of Taşucu in the Silifke district of Türkiye's Mersin Province. There were 267 people on board. Of these, 239 were rescued, 27 died, and one person remains missing.

articles.summary: Supreme Court Chief Justice Cho Hee-dae arrives for work at the Supreme Court in Seoul, Tuesday
articles.body: Supreme Court Chief Justice Cho Hee-dae arrives for work at the Supreme Court in Seoul, Tuesday. Yonhap An international legal association voiced concern over the ruling party's push to impeach the chief justice, urging extreme caution to safeguard judicial independence. In a statement released Thursday, the Law Association for Asia and the Pacific (LAWASIA), acknowledged the constitutional legitimacy of impeachment but stressed the need to uphold fundamental democratic principles. "LAWASIA acknowledges that impeachment is a remedy recognized by the Constitution of the Republic of Korea, and that no person or institution is above the law," the statement read. "LAWASIA emphasises, however, that any action taken by government against the courts must be exercised with extreme caution." LAWASIA represents legal professionals and leading legal associations across some 40 jurisdictions in the Asia-Pacific region. The ruling Democratic Party of Korea (DPK) plans to seek the impeachment of Supreme Court Chief Justice Cho Hee-dae as early as next week. The grounds cited for impeachment include the court's handling of President Lee Jae Myung's election law case, its response to the December 2024 martial law crisis, disputes over judicial appointments and Cho's refusal to testify before the National Assembly. The grounds for impeachment have been disputed, with some critics describing the move as an attempt to silence the judiciary. Any impeachment proceedings must "respect and observe fundamental democratic principles, including the separation of powers and judicial independence," according to the statement. The statement also warned of the potential erosion of public trust in the legal system. "LAWASIA hopes that tensions between the government and the courts can be resolved through constructive dialogue rather than action which risks undermining public confidence in the legal system." LAWASIA adopted the Beijing Principles of the Independence of the Judiciary in 1997, a set of guidelines signed by chief justices from 32 Asia-Pacific countries to safeguard judicial independence. Under Principle 22, judges should be removed from office only on established grounds, such as incapacity, criminal conviction or conduct that makes them unfit to serve. In addition, principle 23 acknowledges that some legal systems allow judges to be removed through parliamentary proceedings but warns that such procedures risk being misused unless reserved for the most serious cases.

Kashagan operator NCOC cleared of asset transaction limits by court
articles.summary: The court overturned a bailiff’s order prohibiting the company from conducting transactions involving its assets, according to the Telegram channel OilGazKZ
articles.body: The Atyrau Regional Court has partially upheld an appeal filed by North Caspian Operating Company (NCOC), the operator of the Kashagan oil field. The court overturned a bailiff’s order prohibiting the company from conducting transactions involving its assets, according to the Telegram channel OilGazKZ . «The Atyrau Regional Court partially granted NCOC’s appeal, ruling that the bailiff’s order prohibiting the company from taking actions involving its assets as part of enforcement proceedings to collect a 2.36 trillion tenge fine was unlawful,» the statement reads. NCOC had challenged five separate orders issued by a bailiff in July as part of enforcement proceedings related to the collection of an environmental fine totaling 2.356 trillion tenge (about $5 billion). Specifically, the company sought to have the following measures declared unlawful: the initiation of enforcement proceedings; the seizure of its real estate and vehicles; and a prohibition on the debtor carrying out certain actions involving its assets. The enforcement proceedings barred NCOC from entering into transactions that could reduce its assets, including the sale, donation, transfer or write-off of property, as well as the assignment of claims. The regional court found that the bailiff’s order did not cite a specific legal basis for the prohibition, explain why the measure was necessary or clearly identify the parties subject to the restriction. The order was also sent to the PSA, the organization representing the state’s interests in the project, for information and implementation. However, the bailiff did not clarify the PSA’s procedural status or establish whether it had the authority to enforce the restrictions. The court therefore concluded that the order was neither lawful nor adequately substantiated and ruled that it should be set aside. The judicial panel noted, however, that the bailiff retains the right to reimpose enforcement measures, provided they comply with legal requirements. The court rejected the remainder of NCOC’s appeal, leaving in force the seizure of the company’s real estate and vehicles, along with the other restrictions imposed as part of the enforcement proceedings. In early September, OilGasKZ reported , citing a response from the Ministry of Justice to an inquiry from Interfax-Kazakhstan, that enforcement proceedings against NCOC had been suspended. Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Justice has denied reports that the collection of a 2.3 trillion tenge environmental fine from NCOC in favor of the state has been terminated. «NCOC has currently appealed the actions of the state bailiff. Therefore, the Atyrau Region Specialized Inter-District Administrative Court has requested the enforcement proceedings,» the ministry said in a statement. The ministry noted that, under subparagraph 13 of Article 42 of Kazakhstan’s Law «On Enforcement Proceedings and the Status of Enforcement Agents,» enforcement proceedings are suspended while the relevant materials are before a court, until the court returns them. Therefore, efforts to collect the funds from NCOC on behalf of the state will continue in accordance with the procedure established by law.

articles.title: Uzbekistan presents disability rights experience at CIS meeting
articles.body: Tashkent, Uzbekistan (UzDaily.uz) — Uzbekistan presented its experience in protecting the rights of persons with disabilities at the seventh meeting of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) Human Rights Commission, held in Minsk. Uzbekistan was represented by Mirzatillo Tillabayev, a member of the Commission and First Deputy Director of the National Human Rights Centre of Uzbekistan. The meeting was chaired by Yevgenia Paramonova, Belarus's representative to the CIS Human Rights Commission and Head of the Main Directorate for Criminal and Judicial Supervision at the Prosecutor General's Office of Belarus. Representatives of Armenia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Russia, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan took part in the meeting in a hybrid format, alongside representatives of the CIS Executive Committee and its structural divisions. Participants heard country reports on the observance of the rights of persons with disabilities in the Commission's member states. The reports were timed to coincide with the CIS Year of Healthcare and the 20th anniversary of the UN General Assembly's adoption of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities on 13 December 2006. Tillabayev outlined Uzbekistan's experience in ensuring and protecting the rights of persons with disabilities. He addressed constitutional guarantees in this area, implementation of the Law on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and the implementation of the UN Convention. Participants showed particular interest in information on the implementation of the action plan marking the Convention's 20th anniversary. They also heard about a special session entitled "20 Years of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities: From Recognition of Rights to Inclusive Societies", scheduled to take place as part of the Fifth Samarkand Human Rights Forum. The Commission also discussed the right to health, in connection with the CIS Year of Healthcare, and the rights of women in the penitentiary system. It reviewed the results of the "Right to Health" creative competition and considered ways to strengthen cooperation on safeguarding the rights and freedoms of migrant workers and their family members, as well as protecting and promoting the rights of older people. Igor Petrishenko, First Deputy Secretary General of the CIS, said that over 35 years the Commonwealth had developed a system of multilateral agreements that formed the basis for interstate dialogue, along with effective cooperation mechanisms covering a wide range of issues. He highlighted cooperation in legal and humanitarian matters, including the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms. During Belarus's 2026 chairmanship, the Commission focused on educational and awareness-raising activities. These included the "Week of Health and Human Rights in the CIS", linked to the Sustainable Development Goals, and the "Right to Health" creative competition, which received hundreds of entries. The meeting approved the Commission's work plan for the coming year, taking into account the designation of 2027 as the CIS Year of Legal Awareness.

"Today's events are yet another reminder that security in the Gulf is a matter of security for us all," she added.

articles.title: Russia slams NATO chief Rutte for Vietnam War analogy on battlefield losses
articles.body:
Russian Security Council Secretary Sergei Shoigu accused NATO chief Mark Rutte of applying double standards in his assessment of Russian casualties in Ukraine, pointing to civilian deaths during the Vietnam War.

In a keynote speech earlier this month, Rutte compared NATO estimates of Russian losses in Ukraine with US casualties during the 14-year Vietnam War.

"In the past few months, Russia has been losing more than 40,000 troops – killed or seriously wounded – every month," Rutte said. "The United States in 14 years, in Vietnam, lost 56,000."

Shoigu hit back in a statement published on Telegram, saying the NATO chief had "sheepishly omitted the fact that the conflict instigated by the US claimed the lives of an estimated 3.4 million Vietnamese, more than 2 million of whom were civilians"

Russia has not given an official death toll among its army since September 2022, when it said almost 6,000 soldiers had been killed in the first six months of fighting – a figure widely seen as a large undercount even at the time.

articles.summary: VIENNA, November 26
articles.body: VIENNA, November 26. /TASS/. NATO’s military activities near Russia’s borders and the involvement of individual alliance countries in attacks on Russian civilian vessels in the Baltic Sea bring the world closer to nuclear war, Russian Permanent Representative to the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) Dmitry Polyansky said on Thursday. The Russian diplomat pointed to NATO’s military activities near Russian borders taking place in parallel with the Freedom Shield 2026 exercises, during which the unblocking of the Suwalki Corridor is being practiced. According to the Russian diplomat, all of this is happening as part of a single operational plan that envisages, on the one hand, the deployment of troops to Ukraine, and, on the other hand, the blockade of the Kaliningrad Region and the creation of an immediate threat to Belarus. Polyansky stated that he had no doubt whatsoever that "the purpose of the exercises near the borders of the Kaliningrad Region is to seize it by means of land, air and sea capabilities." "In other words, a direct path to nuclear war with Russia is being rehearsed," Polyansky continued. "We're also inching closer to that by way of the direct involvement of certain NATO countries in terrorist attacks on Russian civilian vessels in the Baltic Sea," he added. On November 24, Alexander Drozdenko, governor of Russia’s northwestern Leningrad Region, wrote on the Max social media platform, that a cargo vessel en-route to Kaliningrad, Russia’s westernmost exclave, had been attacked by drones in international waters in the Gulf of Finland, three nautical miles from the Russian border. The crew members were evacuated, and the vessel, named Sparta II, was towed to Russia’s second-largest city of St. Petersburg.

Volodymyr Zelensky has warned that Moscow is preparing a “new mass strike” while vowing Kyiv will retaliate against every attack.

Speaking in his nightly video address, Zelensky issued his second such warning this week as Russian forces maintain near-continuous bombardments on Ukrainian cities.

Overnight, Russian ballistic missiles struck Kyiv, wounding seven people and damaging a shopping centre and two other buildings, according to mayor Vitali Klitschko.

Ukraine responded with deep strikes across Russian territory, where Kyiv’s military confirmed overnight drone hits on oil reservoirs at a Transneft facility in the central Bashkortostan region – more than 1,000km from the border.

articles.title: Giant Moscow mural mocks Dutch missile supplies to Ukraine
articles.body:
A giant mural accusing the Netherlands of military aggression has drawn fresh attention near the Dutch embassy in Moscow following diplomatic friction over strikes on the Crimean Bridge.

Painted on an apartment wall, the artwork depicts three tulip-adorned missiles flying over Europe with the slogan: "The flowers of Dutch diplomacy." The Dutch foreign ministry confirmed on Thursday that the mural is not a new reaction to the bridge strikes, noting it was painted months ago.

Tensions between Moscow and The Hague flared last week after Dutch-based aerospace firm Destinus confirmed its missiles were used in Ukraine’s attack on the Crimean Bridge. Two days later, a Russian strike damaged the Dutch embassy in Kyiv, prompting The Hague to summon Russia's ambassador.

Dutch foreign minister Tom Berendsen has rejected claims that arms exports make the Netherlands a party to the war, dismissing Moscow’s warnings as an attempt to "stoke fear" and undermine support for Kyiv.

editorialRejections.title: Moldovan energy minister says Vulcanesti–Chisinau line prevents nationwide blackout in Moldova, after Russian attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure
editorialRejections.summary: The line automatically absorbed disruptions in the regional electricity system, while consumers of Moldova experienced only minor fluctuations
editorialRejections.reason: Ukraine coverage requires an international news source
editorialRejections.body: Moldovan energy minister says Vulcanesti–Chisinau line prevents nationwide blackout in Moldova, after Russian attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure The new Vulcanesti–Chisinau power line has prevented a possible nationwide blackout in Moldova, following Russian attacks on energy infrastructure in the Odesa region. The line automatically absorbed disruptions in the regional electricity system, while consumers of Moldova experienced only minor fluctuations. Energy Minister Dorin Junghietu made statements to this effect during the In Context programme on Moldova 1 TV channel. According to the minister, the attacks took place last Friday, at about 10:30 and the city of Odesa was left practically without electricity. Under these circumstances, the new electricity transmission infrastructure played an important role in maintaining the stability of the national system. “As you know, on that day, Odesa was practically left without electricity, and we felt that shock only as a fluctuation. The national electricity system managed to cope precisely because the Vulcanesti–Chisinau power line had been commissioned and automatically absorbed that potential shock,” Dorin Junghietu said. The minister emphasized that, without the new line, the consequences for Moldova could have been much more serious, with a high risk of a widespread interruption of electricity supplies. “If we had still been using the old Isaccea–Vulcanesti–Kuchurgan line, we would have experienced a power outage. (...) Under the old configuration, there was a very high probability that we would have faced some kind of blackout,” the official said. Dorin Junghietu noted that risks to Moldova’s energy security persist, which is why the government ruled to move from a state of emergency to an alert status in the energy sector, without abandoning rapid-response mechanisms. He also said that Moldova continued to operate within an electricity system integrated with Ukraine’s, and that security developments in the region may affect energy supplies. “We must have mechanisms for rapid intervention in various scenarios, as was the case throughout the current year. (...) Following the attacks that took place in Ukraine during the past week, the Ukrainians set their export capacity to zero. Therefore, they are no longer commercially exporting a single megawatt of electricity,” the minister specified. At present, Moldova is meeting its electricity needs through imports from the Romanian market, particularly during peak hours, to compensate for insufficient domestic production. The Vulcanesti–Chisinau power line, approximately 157 kilometers long and with a capacity of 400 kV, was inaugurated and energized on November 8, 2026. It enables electricity to be transmitted from Romania directly to the center of the country, without passing through the Kuchurgan energy hub. Two other major interconnections are in preparation: the Balti–Suceava line, for which a contract worth 17.5 million euros has been signed, and Straseni–Gutinas, a project estimated at 130 million dollars and financed by the United States, the completion of which is planned for 2032. Ukraine’s energy infrastructure continues to come under Russian attacks, while electricity generation and transmission capacities remain affected. According to an assessment published by the International Energy Agency on November 4, 2026, attacks during the previous winter damaged or destroyed 8.5 GW of electricity generation capacity, while power outages affecting the population reached nearly 12 hours a day in last February. The IEA warns that new attacks on power plants, electricity grids and gas infrastructure continue to pose a risk of energy shortages in next winter too. According to a joint assessment conducted by the government of Ukraine, the World Bank, the European Union, and the United Nations, published on February 23, 2026, total direct damages in Ukraine exceeded 195 billion dollars as of December 31, 2025, while the energy sector recorded an approximately 21-per cent increase in damaged or destroyed assets compared with the previous assessment. The energy sector’s reconstruction and recovery needs are estimated at almost 91 billion dollars. editorialRejections.title: Trump adds Ukraine to warning against expanding war, diverging from joint NATO statement.
editorialRejections.reason: US coverage requires an international or US news source
editorialRejections.body: U.S. President Donald Trump departed from a published joint statement with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte on Nov. 26, adding Ukraine to a warning against expanding the war that was originally directed solely at Russia. The change comes amid growing concerns among European allies over the geographical expansion of Russia's war against Ukraine, following recent Russian airspace violations in Poland and a Ukrainian strike on a Russian warship in the Mediterranean Sea. Trump and Rutte met at the U.S. president's Mar-a-Lago residence in Florida on Nov. 25, with Russia's war against Ukraine and the conflict in Iran among the primary topics of discussion. In the joint statement released following the meeting, the two leaders emphasized "the importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war." Hours later, Trump published his own version of the statement on Truth Social , referring to "the importance of Russia and Ukraine avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the War." A NATO official speaking on condition of anonymity told Politico that both sides had agreed to the original statement, indicating that Trump had subsequently changed the wording unilaterally. The White House did not respond to Politico's request for comment. In a separate social media post on Nov. 26, Trump said he had urged Russian President Vladimir Putin to end military aggression across Europe during their meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 19. Trump also expressed optimism about the possibility of reaching a peace agreement between Ukraine and Russia. The revised wording comes as European leaders grapple with the risk of the war spreading beyond Ukraine's borders. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul separately warned against the geographical expansion of the war on Nov. 26, while reaffirming their countries' support for Ukraine. President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed on Nov. 23 that Ukrainian forces had sunk the Russian corvette Merkury in the Mediterranean Sea off the coast of Benghazi, Libya. Meanwhile, a series of Russian airspace violations in Poland has heightened security concerns among NATO allies, with Warsaw raising the possibility of NATO intercepting Russian missiles over Ukrainian territory.

editorialRejections.title: Trump Revises NATO Statement, Adds Ukraine to Escalation Warning
editorialRejections.reason: US coverage requires an international or US news source
editorialRejections.body: US President Donald Trump has unilaterally revised a joint statement with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, extending to Ukraine a warning originally directed exclusively at Russia against expanding its war. The change came hours after the White House and NATO released an agreed statement following Wednesday’s meeting between Trump and Rutte at the US president’s Mar-a-Lago residence in Florida. The original statement , published by NATO on Thursday, Nov. 26, emphasized the importance of “Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war” and securing a peaceful resolution as quickly as possible. However, in his subsequent post on Truth Social, Trump altered the wording to emphasize the importance of “Russia and Ukraine avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the War.” Both versions called for a swift peace settlement, but Trump’s revision extended the warning to the country defending itself against Russia’s full-scale invasion. A NATO official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told Politico that the original text had been formally agreed upon by both sides, indicating that Trump had subsequently changed the wording without NATO’s agreement. In additional remarks absent from NATO’s statement, Trump said he had discussed with Rutte his recent meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in China. Trump said he wanted to see Putin “pull back all Military aggression against territories throughout Europe.” The remarks followed last week’s trilateral summit in Shenzhen involving Trump, Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, which ended without a ceasefire announcement for Ukraine. Ahead of that meeting, Trump had publicly referred to the Kremlin leader as his friend.

editorialRejections.body: The number of incidents in the Black Sea has increased nearly tenfold in 2026. Rising tensions in the region have reached NATO's borders, creating a direct risk of drawing the Alliance and the United States into the war, CBS News reports.According to NATO military spokesperson Colonel Martin O'Donnell, fewer than 50 incidents were recorded in the Black Sea in 2025, while this year the number has reached between 400 and 500. As a result, the Black Sea has become even more dangerous for seafarers than the Strait of Hormuz amid the confrontation between the United States and Iran. Since the beginning of the year, at least 40 crew members have been killed in the Black Sea, compared with 25 in the Strait of Hormuz. O'Donnell emphasized that the region is critical to global trade, particularly grain and fuel supplies, and that any disruption to food and energy flows would have global consequences, affecting the United States as well. Meanwhile, NATO's Black Sea member states — Romania, Bulgaria, and Türkiye — are finding it increasingly difficult to monitor their maritime borders. According to Romanian Navy Captain Mihai Iordache, the Romanian fleet is operating at the limits of its capacity, constantly neutralizing explosive hazards using divers and underwater drones. Four years ago, we were ready for one drifting mine, and right now we are ready for tens of drifting drones. We don't have enough people, personnel, or equipment to deal with all the commercial ships and all the drones that we have, Iordache said. Amid growing threats on NATO's eastern flank, including the recent crash of Russian cruise missiles in southeastern Poland and repeated drone incursions into the Alliance's airspace, NATO officials in Brussels reaffirmed their readiness to defend allies under Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty. I would say that there should be no doubt about NATO's willingness and ability to act, NATO spokesperson Martin O'Donnell emphasized. Maritime security and establishing a ceasefire in the Black Sea remain among the most challenging issues in the negotiation process. Kyiv previously stated that Ukraine expects pressure from several countries that directly depend on maritime supplies to encourage Russia to agree to a ceasefire in the Black Sea. Meanwhile, as Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan explained, Russia refuses to agree to a separate ceasefire in the Black Sea without signing a comprehensive, long-term peace agreement with Ukraine, while the negotiation process itself remains effectively deadlocked over the territorial issue of Donbas.

editorialRejections.title: Could the Black Sea pull the U.S. into war in Europe? The Russia-Ukraine war is spilling into the Black Sea, where violent incidents have surged, running right up to NATO's doorstep.
editorialRejections.summary: In 2025, for example, we saw fewer than 50 incidents in the Black Sea
editorialRejections.reason: Question headlines are excluded
editorialRejections.body: Constanța, Romania – Out on the Black Sea, the Romanian Navy is always on the lookout for the deadly debris of a war it isn't fighting.It's a front of the Russia-Ukraine war that most people rarely see. It runs right up to NATO's doorstep and sometimes crosses into its waters — threatening to pull the alliance, and therefore the United States, into the war.Incidents involving drones, mines and commercial ships are surging in the Black Sea, NATO military spokesperson Colonel Martin O'Donnell told CBS News."In 2025, for example, we saw fewer than 50 incidents in the Black Sea. This year alone, we're talking four to five hundred," he said.The roughly tenfold increase threatens a major artery of global grain and fuel shipments and has made the waterway deadlier than the Strait of Hormuz, a flashpoint in the U.S.-Iran war, with both sides trying to enforce blockades on the chokepoint to exert economic pressure on the other.Twenty-five sailors have been killed in the strait this year, according to the International Maritime Organization, while at least 40 have been killed in the Black Sea in the same period, according to the International Transport Workers' Federation."I would say the Black Sea is just as important, and then depending on who you talk to, some might argue could perhaps even be more important … in terms of global trade," said O'Donnell.Any imbalance in the flow of fuel and food "can have global implications that can impact America just as much as it can any of the nations here," he said.And this maritime front stretches beyond the Black Sea.Over the weekend, Ukraine said it struck an advanced Russian warship and a cargo ship that then drifted, on fire, into the waters of NATO member Finland.On Sunday, Ukraine said it sank a Russian warship docked in Libya.Three of the six countries bordering the Black Sea are NATO members — Romania, Bulgaria and Turkey.But as Romanian Navy Captain Mihai Iordache explains, defending those borders is nothing like defending them on land."We do not have a fence into the Black Sea to state this is our border, that is the other border," he said.The Romanian Navy is deploying highly specialized divers and drones, scouring the depths for unexploded weapons.All this comes as the pressure on NATO is mounting. On Friday, Poland accused Russia of "intentional provocation" as Russian cruise missiles landed in the country's southeast. Drones have repeatedly entered the airspace of Poland and other NATO countries, mostly near Ukraine but not all, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022.The Article 5 collective defense clause in NATO's founding charter states that an attack on one member is considered an attack on all 32.Asked whether the alliance will defend itself if necessary, O'Donnell told CBS News: "I would say that there should be no doubt on NATO's willingness and ability to act."On the Black Sea, Captain Iordache warns the Romanian Navy is already stretched thin."We don't have enough people, personnel, equipment to deal with all the commercial ships and all the drones that we have," he told CBS News during an embed."Four years ago, we were ready for one drifting mine, and right now we are ready for tens of drifting drones," he said. "So I presume we'll be ready in the future, who knows what the future will bring." "Could be hotter, could be colder, who knows. Let's hope for peace."
